Ardestani Affiliation: Meta Zhan Shu Affiliation: Meta Adnan Aziz Affiliation: Meta Yi Xu Affiliation: Meta Abstract Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) repeatedly alternate between model inference and tool calls, creating long-lived sessions with reusable key-value (KV) states and asynchronous request resumptions. Logical readiness , however, does not ensure efficient admission in a shared serving system. Through direct trace analysis and trace-driven replay, we identify two mismatches: reusable KV states reside across storage tiers and incur unequal computational costs for state preparation , while requests with heterogeneous context lengths can decode inefficiently together. Our central insight is that exploiting admission flexibility can improve serving performance while preserving request progress. We present Coda , a coding-agent serving system that realizes this insight through a readiness-informed admission layer incorporating two mechanisms. Tiered-Aging state admission exploits bounded flexibility in admission order to improve admission efficiency and preserve request progress. Compatibility-Aware execution admission exploits flexibility in attention grouping within each model iteration to reduce mixed-context interference and improve shared decoding efficiency. For multi-worker configurations, Coda introduces a separate routing layer that considers KV-state residency, worker load, and request-to-worker context-length compatibility to guide efficient request placement. We evaluate Coda across different models and workloads against state-of-the-art coding-agent serving systems and vLLM. Across the single-worker and multi-worker experiments, Coda improves output-token and SLO-compliant throughput by 20.3% and 70.5% on average, with peak gains of 29.3% and 140.2%. 1 Introduction LLM coding agents extend software automation from code generation to multi-step development workflows, including repository-level repair, code editing, environment configuration, and test execution [ 23 , 3 , 26 , 30 ] . Systems such as OpenAI Codex [ 17 ] , Claude Code [ 1 ] , and Cursor [ 5 ] support these workflows through integrated model inference and tool execution. As Figure 1 illustrates, concurrent sessions repeatedly pause for tools, resume asynchronously, and accumulate context across model rounds [ 21 , 24 ] . A request becomes logically ready when user input arrives or a tool return enables its session to continue. Logical readiness determines whether a request may proceed, but it does not determine whether that request should be prepared next or how efficiently it will share GPU execution with other ready requests. Admitting a request commits GPU resources and changes how other requests share those resources. Two characteristics of coding-agent workloads make this distinction particularly important. Figure 1 : Illustrative multi-session coding-agent workflows. Independent sessions alternate between model inference and tool execution. Tool calls return asynchronously, and their outputs extend subsequent model inputs, causing session contexts to grow at different rates. First, readiness does not imply equal computational cost for preparation. Long-lived coding-agent sessions accumulate reusable interaction histories across successive model and tool invocations. Preserving the KV cache avoids repeated prefix computation, but the aggregate KV state of concurrent sessions can exceed available GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, motivating storage across HBM, CPU DRAM, and lower storage tiers [ 16 , 18 ] . During tool-induced idle periods, memory pressure may evict a session’s KV state from HBM before its next request becomes ready [ 24 , 21 , 12 ] . Consequently, equally ready requests can require substantially different preparation: one may reuse HBM-resident state, whereas another requires restoration, storage access, or prefix recomputation. In our trace-driven replay (§ 3 ), 24.45% of resumed requests are not HBM-ready but account for 42.45% of total startup computational cost . Admission based on arrival order or reusable-prefix availability alone can therefore allow computationally expensive state preparation to delay several computationally inexpensive session continuations. Second, readiness does not imply efficient shared execution. Long-lived coding-agent sessions accumulate context at different rates, while asynchronous tool returns bring sessions at different stages back into execution [ 30 , 21 ] . Consequently, short-context requests frequently execute alongside requests with substantially larger KV states. Although each request is ready to proceed, heterogeneous context lengths can reduce attention-kernel efficiency during shared decoding [ 2 ] . In our trace-driven replay (§ 3 ), 82.84% of multi-request decode iterations have a largest-to-smallest context-length ratio of at least 4 × \times . For pure-decode iterations, at fixed request count and total context-token volume, the observed context composition incurs a 25.95% higher median computational cost per iteration than a near-uniform composition. Admission based only on individual readiness can therefore create a heterogeneous active population; treating that population as a single attention group leaves context-length compatibility unaddressed. Exploiting these opportunities is challenging. Prioritizing requests with low computational costs of state preparation can reduce blocking, but may repeatedly bypass sessions whose KV states reside in lower tiers. Conversely, strict ready-time order prevents reordering-based bypass but sacrifices this efficiency opportunity. Similarly, organizing heterogeneous contexts into separate attention groups can improve attention efficiency, but additional launches and smaller groups may outweigh the benefit; this tradeoff must be assessed online as the active population changes. In multi-worker configurations, context-compatible placement can also conflict with KV affinity and load balance. Logical readiness should determine eligibility, but not admission order or execution grouping. Our approach exploits bounded flexibility between readiness and execution to reorder state preparation and reorganize attention groups. In this paper, admission is twofold: state admission determines which logically ready request is prepared next, while execution admission determines how the current participating requests are organized for execution. These two decisions expose flexibility in admission order and execution grouping: Flexibility in admission order. Admission can account for differences in the computational costs of KV-state preparation when selecting which logically ready request is prepared next. Bounded reordering can improve admission efficiency while guarding against indefinite bypass. Flexibility in execution grouping. Admission can account for context-length compatibility when organizing the participating requests for attention execution. Compatibility-aware grouping can improve shared decoding efficiency when its computational savings exceed the computational cost of additional execution groups. Existing systems improve coding-agent serving through cache management, session placement, and resource coordination. CacheWise combines prefix-aware scheduling based on additional KV-block demand with predictive KV-cache eviction informed by tool calls [ 21 ] . SMetric uses session reuse and worker load to guide request routing [ 22 ] , while MORI manages GPU and CPU residency through relative program idleness and tier admission [ 24 ] . AlignedServe instead forms batches from waiting requests with similar KV-cache lengths [ 2 ] . Existing systems therefore address individual aspects of residency, placement, or context-aware batching, but do not jointly provide bounded preparation-aware ordering and within-iteration attention grouping for asynchronously resuming coding-agent sessions. We present Coda , a coding-agent serving system that decouples logical readiness from physical GPU execution through a readiness-informed admission layer. Tiered-Aging state admission realizes bounded admission-order flexibility by combining the computational cost of KV-state preparation, waiting age, and a progress guard. Compatibility-Aware execution admission realizes execution-grouping flexibility by applying context-compatible attention groups only when conservative predicted computational savings exceed their additional computational overhead. For multi-worker configurations, a separate routing layer considers context-length compatibility only within KV-affinity and load safeguards. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Contribution 1: We characterize coding-agent workloads through direct trace analysis and replay (§ 3 ). We examine how changing KV-state residency creates unequal computational costs for state preparation , and how uneven context growth and tool returns create heterogeneous decode contexts. These findings show why logical readiness alone is insufficient and motivate flexible admission order and execution grouping . Contribution 2: We design and implement Coda with two admission mechanisms (§ 4 ): Tiered-Aging state admission (§ 4.2 ) and Compatibility-Aware execution admission (§ 4.3 ). A complementary routing layer supports multi-worker configurations (§ 5 ). We integrate these mechanisms as an orchestration layer connected to the inference backend (§ 6 ). Contribution 3: We evaluate Coda across models and workloads in single-worker and multi-worker configurations (§ 7 ). Compared with state-of-the-art coding-agent serving systems and a vLLM baseline, Coda improves single-worker output-token throughput by 17.5% on average and up to 23.9%, and SLO-compliant throughput by 96.1% on average and up to 140.2%. In the multi-worker experiments, output-token throughput improves by 23.1% on average and up to 29.3%, while SLO-compliant throughput improves by 45.0% on average and up to 59.0%. Component ablations and runtime analysis further identify the contributions of Tiered-Aging state admission, Compatibility-Aware execution admission, and routing to serving performance. 2 Background and Motivation Coding-agent serving background. Coding-agent workflows interleave model inference with development tools for repository inspection, code modification, command execution, and testing [ 26 , 23 ] . A session comprises multiple dependent model requests, with tool outputs incorporated into the input of subsequent requests [ 27 , 21 ] . Each model request involves prefill computation for input tokens and iterative decoding for output generation. Retaining the corresponding key-value (KV) state allows subsequent requests to reuse the session prefix rather than repeatedly compute it [ 6 , 15 ] . Unlike isolated inference requests, coding-agent sessions retain growing interaction histories and repeatedly pause for tool execution, producing long-lived KV states and asynchronous resumptions [ 30 , 14 , 4 ] . Concurrent sessions compete for GPU memory, motivating KV storage across GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and lower storage tiers [ 15 , 18 ] . Meanwhile, serving engines combine requests into batches, so requests from different session stages may decode together [ 13 , 28 ] . Admission therefore affects more than an individual request: admission order determines which request’s state-preparation work occurs next and shapes which contexts execute concurrently . Figure 2 : Illustrative example of multi-tier KV storage. Lower tiers provide larger storage capacity. HBM-resident KV is directly accessible for decoding, whereas DRAM-resident KV requires GPU restoration and SSD-resident KV first requires loading into DRAM. Multi-tier KV storage. GPU serving systems extend KV-cache storage across GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSDs to balance access efficiency and capacity across the hierarchy [ 19 , 6 , 18 ] . GPU HBM provides high-bandwidth access to KV state during model execution, but its limited capacity must also accommodate model weights and runtime buffers [ 13 , 6 ] . CPU DRAM provides additional capacity for reusable KV state, while SSDs offer a larger-capacity storage tier [ 15 ] . As illustrated in Figure 2 , these tiers differ in the work required to reuse cached state: HBM-resident KV can be accessed directly, CPU-resident KV requires transfer to the GPU, and SSD-resident KV additionally requires storage I/O [ 6 , 15 ] . If reusable state is unavailable, the corresponding prefix must be recomputed. Restoring cached state also does not eliminate prefill computation for newly appended input tokens. Consequently, retaining a reusable prefix avoids redundant computation, but its current storage location still affects the computational cost of resuming a request. Systems for coding-agent serving. Recent systems exploit session structure, tool behavior, and KV reuse to improve coding-agent serving. CacheWise combines prefix-aware scheduling with predictive KVCache eviction: it prioritizes requests requiring fewer additional KV blocks and uses tool information to predict relative future reuse for eviction decisions [ 21 ] . SMetric introduces balanced session-centric scheduling, using actual local-prefix hits to preserve session locality and load-aware guards to prevent overloaded workers from retaining requests solely for reuse [ 22 ] . MORI derives relative program idleness from inference and tool-call timings, coordinating KV-state residency and program admission across GPU and CPU tiers [ 24 ] . ThunderAgent represents multi-turn workflows as LLM programs and coordinates program execution through memory-pressure-aware pause and restore decisions, together with tool-environment management [ 12 ] . For interactive LLM serving, Bidaw prioritizes SSD KV loading according to KV size and waiting time to reduce storage-induced request blocking [ 7 ] . CacheWise does not combine tier-specific preparation time with a waiting bound. SMetric does not consider context-length compatibility, and MORI, ThunderAgent, and Bidaw do not optimize within-iteration attention grouping. None of these systems jointly addresses admission order and execution organization. AlignedServe groups requests with similar prefix lengths by controlling which requests enter the next batch, potentially delaying requests and requiring starvation handling; Coda instead keeps the participating request set unchanged and reorganizes only its attention computation [ 2 ] . These systems establish the importance of locality, residency, and program-level resource control in coding-agent and interactive LLM serving. Coda instead places admission flexibility at the center of its design, which is based on careful coding-agent workload characterizations and jointly considers admission order and execution grouping within a unified admission layer. Motivation. In coding-agent serving, ready requests differ in both the work required to prepare their KV states and their context-length compatibility for shared decoding. These differences make admission consequential for shared serving performance. A returning session may require substantial KV restoration and prefill work, while another can proceed with little preparation. Meanwhile, asynchronous resumptions bring requests with different context lengths into shared decoding, where their execution efficiency depends on how they are organized together. Logical readiness therefore leaves two important choices: which ready request should have its KV state prepared next, and how the participating requests should be organized for execution . Understanding whether these choices offer meaningful performance opportunities requires careful characterization of the underlying coding-agent workload behavior. The following section characterizes KV-state residency and startup computational costs ( Findings 1-3 ), within-worker context composition and decode efficiency ( Findings 4-7 ), and cross-worker context composition ( Finding 8 ). These findings motivate our state-admission, execution-admission, and routing mechanisms, respectively. 3 Coding-Agent Workload and System Characterization Trace and replay methodology. We characterize the complete TraceLab corpus [ 30 ] , which contains 357,161 model rounds, 432,510 tool calls, and 4,281 physical sessions. We obtain request- and session-level properties directly from the trace. For runtime state not recorded by TraceLab, including physical KV-tier placement, concurrent request populations, decode iterations, and worker assignments, we use policy-neutral trace-driven replays that preserve request tokens, session order, and observed tool-call intervals. Specifically, we use a common hierarchy replay with a 30-minute warm-up followed by a two-hour measurement interval. The evaluation configuration consists of four A100-80GB workers, each with 33.91 GiB of usable HBM KV-cache capacity, 384 GiB of shared DRAM, and a 2-TiB SSD tier. Reusable KV states are distributed across storage tiers. At the end of the measurement interval, HBM holds 21 resident KV-state copies (129.5 GiB), DRAM holds 57 (383.4 GiB), and SSD holds 316 (2,047.3 GiB). These copy counts overlap because the hierarchy maintains lower-tier shadows. During the interval, 39,271 requests resume existing sessions after user input or tool-call returns. Among them, 9,601 (24.45%) are not HBM-ready: 6,769 (17.24%) require CPU-to-GPU restoration from DRAM, 2,763 (7.04%) require SSD-to-CPU loading followed by GPU restoration, and 69 (0.18%) require prefix recomputation. The SSD remains near capacity and performs 1,858 evictions. Lower-tier restoration generates 64,517.2 GiB of CPU-to-HBM traffic, including 15,705.3 GiB that first crosses the SSD-to-CPU link. Finding 1. Reusable coding-agent KV state spans the storage hierarchy. A reusable prefix may reside below HBM and require substantial state movement before execution. KV-state residency changes continuously. Asynchronous tool-call returns repeatedly reactivate different coding-agent sessions, changing which reusable KV states reside in each storage tier. Between adjacent 10-minute boundaries, 80.00-100.00% of HBM-resident session identities, 79.59-91.67% of DRAM-resident identities, and 34.95-53.24% of SSD-resident identities are replaced. Thus, KV-state residency is a transient property rather than a fixed session attribute. Finding 2. Reusable KV-state residency changes continuously as asynchronous tool-call returns reshape storage-tier residency. Request startup computational costs vary across KV-state preparation paths. For each request in the trace replay, startup computational cost captures the KV-state movement and prefill work required before decoding can begin. The p50/p95 startup computational costs are 0.320/3.214 s for HBM-ready requests, 0.623/3.820 s for requests requiring DRAM restoration, 1.760/12.633 s for requests requiring SSD loading, and 8.797/45.466 s for requests requiring prefix recomputation. Although only 7.21% of resumed requests require SSD loading or recomputation, these paths contribute 23.03% of total startup computational cost. DRAM restoration is required by 17.24% of resumed requests and contributes another 19.42%. Across successive 10-minute trace-replay windows, requests collectively incur 3,238-4,266 s of startup computational cost. The HBM-ready, DRAM-restoration, and SSD-loading/recomputation paths contribute 51.22-71.40%, 11.79-24.78%, and 16.81-27.78% of this computational cost, respectively. Figure 3 summarizes the distribution and temporal composition of request startup computational cost. Figure 3 : Left: p50 (circle) and p95 (diamond) startup computational costs, including KV-state movement and prefill, for resumed requests grouped by their required KV-state preparation path. Right: each stacked bar shows the share of total startup work attributable to HBM-ready, DRAM-restoration, and SSD-loading/recomputation paths for each successive 10-minute trace-replay interval. Finding 3. Coding-agent request startup computational costs vary substantially across KV-state preparation paths, and each path’s contribution to the system’s startup computational cost changes over time. Session context growth and tool-call durations vary widely. Across 3,801 multi-round sessions, the ratio between the maximum and first-round context lengths is 4.45 × \times at p50, 13.96 × \times at p90, and 37.77 × \times at p99; 54.64% of sessions grow by at least 4 × \times . Tool-call duration also varies widely. Among 419,735 completed tool calls, duration is 0.209 s at p50, 8.866 s at p90, 30.013 s at p95, and 180.002 s at p99. Figure 4 summarizes these session-growth and tool-return distributions. Figure 4 : Left: maximum-to-first context-growth ratio across session percentiles for 3,801 multi-round sessions. Right: cumulative share of total tool-call elapsed time contributed by 419,735 completed positive-duration tool calls ranked from longest to shortest. Dashed diagonal: uniform contribution. Finding 4. Uneven context growth and widely varying tool-call durations cause coding-agent sessions to reach different context lengths and resume execution asynchronously. Context lengths vary widely within decode iterations. We examine each context vector immediately after the standard continuous batching planner forms a decode iteration. Across 102,809 multi-request iterations, the largest materialized context is at least 2 × \times the smallest in 99.76% of iterations, at least 4 × \times in 82.84%, and at least 8 × \times in 30.02%. The largest-to-smallest context-length ratio is 6.32 × \times at p50 and 19.69 × \times at p95, while the context-length CV is 0.58 at p50 and 0.93 at p95.
